name: Pseudonymization procedure implemented
evidenceGuidance: Provide evidence of your pseudonymization procedure. Guidance: The GDPR defines pseudonymization as a process to render data unattributable to a specific data subject unless additional information (that is kept separately) is used to reidentify the subject(s). Pseudonymization makes data identifiable if necessary, yet inaccessible to unauthorized users and allows entities to lower the risk of a potential data breach and safeguard personal data at-rest and in-transit. A pseudonym is still considered to be personal data according to the GDPR since the process should theoretically be reversible. The applicability of pseudonymization depends on a number of factors, including risk of the processed data, method of processing, and security controls in place for the data. Vanta recommends reaching out to Privacy counsel for more clarity on this topic.

name: Proof of media/device disposal
evidenceGuidance: Provide evidence that physical media is disposed of properly through certificates of sanitization or destruction. Guidance: NIST 800-88 provides guidelines for media sanitization, including methods and techniques for differing types of media. As an example, PCI DSS Requirement 9 requires cardholder data on electronic media be rendered unrecoverable when deleted such as through a secure wipe program or be physically destroyed. There are many reputable companies which provide physical media destruction services and will issue certificates of destruction upon completion, such as Data Destruction Corporation. In lieu of a third-party performing data destruction, you can perform it internally and leverage the following sample certificate: Sample Certificate of Destruction: Google docs template / Docx template. Note: Test may be marked as not relevant if no media disposal is required and has not occurred. Implementation guidance Identify any physical media (e.g., hard drives, USBs, backup tapes) that must be sanitized or destroyed due to data lifecycle policies, PCI DSS requirements, or regulatory mandates. If destruction is handled internally, use the Google Docs Template or Word Template to document the destruction. If handled externally, request a formal certificate of destruction from the service provider. File all completed certificates in a centralized compliance repository and reference relevant standards (e.g., NIST 800-88) on each form to demonstrate audit alignment. Evidence collection To collect this evidence, gather documentation that verifies proper sanitization or destruction of physical media according to recognized security standards. Obtain certificates from external destruction vendors that include media type, disposal method, date of destruction, and authorized personnel or witnesses If performed internally, complete and sign destruction certificates using approved internal templates. Ensure the evidence references compliance with NIST 800-88 and, where applicable, PCI DSS Requirement 9. Retain supporting logs, chain-of-custody documentation, or internal policy references to validate the integrity of the process.

name: Firewall reviewed annually
evidenceGuidance: Upload evidence detailing the result of the annual firewall ruleset review. Examples of the content of the firewall review report are: Reviewer Information and Timing: Who conducted the review and when the review was conducted. Review Coverage: Detail the firewalls, networks, or segments that were examined. Ruleset Overview: The total number of rules reviewed. Any grouping or segmentation used within the ruleset (e.g., by function, network segment, or application). Rule Description: For each rule or a representative sample of rules, include: Rule ID, Action (allow/block), Source and destination IP addresses, Ports and protocols involved. Purpose/Justification: Provide an explanation of the intended function of each rule and its necessity for business operations or security posture. Compliance Status: Evaluate the compliance of each rule with organizational policies and best practices in firewall management. Identify any deviations or areas of concern. Recommendations: Based on the findings, suggest actions for each rule or set of rules. Recommendations may include: Modification of existing rules to tighten security without impacting necessary business functions. Deletion of obsolete, unused, or overly permissive rules. Note: This evidence is only required for admin users of tools that have not been connected to Vanta via the integrations page. A template can be found here: Google docs template Implementation guidance Identify and inventory systems not integrated with Vanta. Engage system owners and administrators to obtain or generate current reports of administrative users, ensuring the list captures business partners, service accounts, vendors, third-party accounts, contractors, and employees. Establish a routine process for updating these lists by defining clear responsibilities and review cycles, documenting role changes and verifying the removal of unnecessary access. Consolidate the updated lists and supporting documentation into an accessible evidence package, and schedule periodic reviews to ensure ongoing accuracy and compliance. Evidence collection To collect evidence for the control of maintaining privileged user lists, you would typically gather documentation that reflects current access roles and responsibilities. Request a current list or report of administrative users from system administrators. Verify that the list includes all relevant user types, such as business partners, service accounts, vendors, third-party accounts, contractors, and employees. name: Customer account access request
evidenceGuidance: Provide an example of a recent access request and approval flow, such as through a Jira ticket or email, to grant employee access to customer data in your application. Guidance: Best practice is to track and document data access requests through tickets or utilization of an identity access management tool (IAM). However, if tickets or a data access management tool is not being used, email threads and/or a manual access request form may also be acceptable. Here's a sample access request form: Google docs template / Docx template. Implementation guidance Set up a secure customer submission process using a support ticket system, web form, or dedicated email channel that logs each request with details like date, customer identifier (sanitized), and request type. Develop and implement an internal process where each request is validated (e.g., verifying identity through multi-factor checks), tracked, approved by a designated support agent or team, and followed by record-keeping of actions taken. Create or update standard operating procedures (SOPs) and checklists that outline each step of the process, ensuring that all evidence—including submission timestamps and resolution details—is stored in an auditable, secure repository. Evidence collection To collect evidence of customer account access request handling, provide records that demonstrate secure, traceable, and consistent processes. Submit a support ticket, form submission, or email request from a customer requesting account access or changes (e.g., password reset, account ownership transfer). Include internal handling records showing how the request was validated and fulfilled (e.g., verification steps, approval, response). Ensure the evidence shows the date, requester, responsible support agent or team, and resolution outcome. Provide documentation of any standard operating procedures (SOPs) or checklists used to manage such requests securely. Sanitize any personal data in the submission before sharing evidence.

name: Version control system access review
evidenceGuidance: Please provide evidence of the last access review performed on your version control system(s). If native logging isn’t enough, explore integrations or simple scripts to capture these events automatically. Establish a periodic review process where a designated team member verifies the logs, ensuring all access rights and changes are documented. This process should culminate in a formal review report that aligns with your organization’s access control policies. Document the review process—including roles, steps taken, and evidence collected—and securely archive the reports. This documentation not only aids in demonstrating compliance but also supports ongoing process improvements. Evidence collection To collect evidence for the access review of a version control system, gather documentation that details user access rights, any changes made, and the date of the review. Obtain the most recent access review report or log file from the version control system. Ensure the document includes a list of users with access, their access levels, and any modifications to access rights. Verify that the document is dated and reflects the latest review conducted. Confirm that the report aligns with the organization's access control policies.

name: Autoscaling

Retrieve configuration settings or screenshots from your cloud environment (AWS, Azure, GCP) confirming autoscaling is active. Export logs or reports from your autoscaling service that show thresholds, usage patterns, or trigger events. Capture a full screenshot including the timestamp. Save and archive the image for audit reference.

name: Secure configuration baselines developed
evidenceGuidance: Provide evidence of documented configuration baselines based on industry standards such as CIS, NIST 800 series, NIST STIGs, etc.) for all in-scope systems such as: Operating Systems Cloud Infrastructure and Services Servers or Compute Instances Endpoint Software Network Infrastructure (Firewalls, VPCs, Security Groups) Databases Acceptable evidence can include: A configuration baseline document outlining security settings for each in-scope system. Screenshots or reports from security tools (e.g., CIS Benchmark scans, AWS Security Hub findings) showing compliance with baseline standards. Documentation of access controls, logging configurations, and system monitoring settings. A simple spreadsheet listing key configurations and security settings applied across systems. Implementation Guidance for Startups: If you don’t have a mature IT team, start with these steps: Identify what you use – List the technologies you rely on (e.g., AWS, Linux, Windows, databases, firewalls). Use existing templates – Download CIS benchmarks or NIST STIGs relevant to your technology stack. Many security tools (e.g., AWS Security Hub, Microsoft Defender) provide default recommendations. Apply basic hardening – Disable unnecessary services, enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA), enable logging, and restrict admin access. Document in a simple format – A Google Doc or spreadsheet listing key security settings is enough to start. Track what’s configured, who owns it, and when it was last reviewed. Set up alerts & reviews – Use built-in cloud security tools (AWS Config, Azure Security Center) to monitor compliance, and schedule periodic checks (quarterly or biannually) to keep settings up to date. Audit Consideration: During your audit window, be prepared to re-upload evidence for at least a 10% for your interconnected system components, as randomly selected and requested by your auditor. A template can be found here: Google docs template Implementation guidance Identify all in-scope systems and any existing configuration documentation. Determine where security settings, access controls, and logging configurations need to be defined according to industry standards. Create or update configuration baseline documents for each system. Use industry guidelines (e.g., CIS, NIST 800 series, NIST STIGs) to outline secure settings and ensure documentation covers operating systems, cloud infrastructure, servers, endpoints, networks, and databases. Use security tools to regularly scan and assess configurations. Collect and archive tool reports and audit logs that demonstrate compliance, making sure all evidence is current and accessible. Evidence collection To collect this evidence, gather documents and reports showing secure configuration standards. Obtain baseline documents listing secure settings by system type. Collect screenshots or reports from security tools (e.g., AWS Security Hub, CIS scans). Document logging, access control, and system hardening settings. Compile a spreadsheet or simple report tracking what is applied, to what systems, and who owns it. Ensure all evidence is current and reflects actual system configurations.

name: Data Masking
evidenceGuidance: NOTE: This control is optional if Data Masking is not in scope for your audit. Provide evidence demonstrating that data masking is implemented to protect sensitive information from unauthorized access. The evidence should confirm that masking techniques are in place for both structured and unstructured data, in adherence with policy requirements. Logs or reports from databases showing masked values in non-production environments. Screenshots of masked data within applications, reports, or logs demonstrating that sensitive data is obfuscated. Role-based access control (RBAC) settings demonstrating that only authorized users can access unmasked data. Logs showing access attempts and enforcement of data masking rules. Results of data masking effectiveness tests, including screenshots or sample queries showing masked versus unmasked data. Configure the tool by setting up masking rules for the identified data fields, ensuring these rules apply consistently across data formats, and integrate role-based access controls. Validate and document the implementation by capturing screenshots or exporting configuration settings, generating logs that display masked values, and reviewing access controls for authorized users only. Evidence collection To collect evidence of data masking: Gather configuration settings from your masking tools or scripts that apply masking rules to sensitive fields. Capture logs or screenshots showing masked values in staging or analytics environments. Obtain RBAC settings that enforce masking visibility. Export sample test results showing masking was applied and validated.

name: Data restore test
evidenceGuidance: Provide evidence demonstrating that periodic database recovery or restore tests are planned and completed successfully from backups.Acceptable evidence and implementation guidance: Documented Test Plans and Schedules: Outline the frequency and scope of planned database recovery tests. Regular testing ensures that backups can be restored effectively in case of data loss or system failure. Test Execution Records: Maintain records of executed recovery tests, including dates, personnel involved, and outcomes. This documentation demonstrates adherence to the backup policy and the effectiveness of recovery procedures. Validation Reports: After each recovery test, compile reports detailing the validation of post-recovery results, identification of any errors or issues, and corrective actions taken. Regular testing of backup jobs is essential to ensure data availability and to measure recovery times against organizational objectives. Implementation guidance Define and document the backup and restore test plan: Establish clear procedures outlining the frequency, scope, and specific steps for performing data restore tests. Include details like responsible personnel, roles, and a schedule for testing. Execute the restore tests per the plan, keeping detailed records of each test session—including steps taken, issues encountered, and resolutions. Ensure these records capture all relevant data for validation. After each test, generate test results/validation reports confirming that the restore procedures met backup policies and were successful. Use these reports to refine processes and schedule future tests. Evidence collection To collect evidence for the control related to data restore tests, focus on documentation that demonstrates the planning and execution of these tests. Evidence should include test plans, schedules, execution records, and test results/validation reports. Gather test plans and schedules that outline the frequency and scope of restore tests. Collect execution records that detail the steps taken during the tests and any issues encountered. Obtain test results/validation reports that confirm the success of the tests and adherence to backup policies. Ensure documentation is up-to-date and reflects recent test activities.

name: Backups completed for other databases

Evidence that backups are enabled and running as scheduled. Logs or reports confirming successful backup completions over time. If using a third-party or cloud backup service (e.g., AWS Backup, Veeam, Acronis), provide configuration details or reports. Implementation guidance Identify and configure your backup system for each in-scope database by setting up regular backup schedules and ensuring backup settings (e.g., retention policies, versioning) are captured in the management console. Enable logging for all backup activities so that each successful backup run generates a log entry or report; periodically perform restoration tests and document the results. Collect and store evidence such as screenshots or exported configuration files, log excerpts, and test restoration documentation in a centralized repository to demonstrate ongoing compliance. Evidence collection To collect evidence for the control related to backups of databases, focus on gathering technical evidence that demonstrates proper configuration and maintenance of backup systems. Access the backup management console or system to capture screenshots or export settings that show backup configurations. Retrieve logs that confirm successful completion of backups. Document results from restoration tests to verify backup integrity. If third-party services are used, obtain configuration details or reports from the service provider.

name: Change management procedure documentation
evidenceGuidance: Provide evidence that changes to information processing facilities and information systems are managed according to established change management procedures.Acceptable evidence can include: -A documented change management policy outlining procedures for requesting, assessing, approving, implementing, and reviewing changes.-Records of recent change requests and approvals, demonstrating segregation of duties.-Minutes from Change Advisory Board (CAB) meetings where proposed changes were discussed and approved.-Evidence of impact assessments conducted prior to implementing changes, such as risk assessment reports or testing plans.-Documentation showing that operating procedures and user guidelines are reviewed and updated following changes.-Records indicating that business continuity and disaster recovery plans are evaluated and updated to accommodate changes.A template can be found here: Google docs template Implementation guidance Define and document your change management process by creating or formalizing a procedure, standardized templates, and record-keeping procedures to capture change requests, approvals, meeting minutes, impact assessments, and updates to operating procedures, business continuity, and disaster recovery plans. Set up regular reviews (e.g., periodic CAB meetings and impact assessments) to update records and verify that all procedural changes are reflected in related plans; this ongoing practice will help ensure continuous compliance and evidence collection for audits. Evidence collection Collect evidence by gathering documentation that demonstrates adherence to change management procedures for information processing facilities and systems. Obtain documented change management procedure. Collect records of recent change requests and approvals. Gather minutes from Change Advisory Board (CAB) meetings. name: Installed applications monitored
evidenceGuidance: Provide evidence demonstrating that the organization monitors and controls applications installed by users to prevent unauthorized or non-compliant software usage. This applies to both corporate-managed devices and, where applicable, Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) environments. Acceptable evidence can include: Screenshots of Mobile Device Management (MDM) configurations (e.g., Intune, JAMF, Workspace ONE) enforcing application restrictions. Policies showing whitelisting or blacklisting of applications via Active Directory (AD), Group Policy, or Azure Modern Management. Endpoint protection settings that detect and block unauthorized software. Logs or reports from security tools (e.g., Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne) showing application activity and enforcement actions. Alerts or notifications triggered when unapproved applications are installed. Records of enforcement actions, such as blocked application attempts or incident reports related to unauthorized software. BYOD-Specific Controls (if applicable): Conditional access policies that limit corporate data access based on device compliance status. Document these policies so users and administrators understand what software is allowed. Leverage existing management tools: Configure your Mobile Device Management (MDM) and endpoint protection systems to enforce these application policies. Adjust settings to automatically block unauthorized installations and log all changes related to installed applications. Set up continuous monitoring and documentation: Enable logging within your security tools to track application installations and any enforcement actions taken. Regularly review these logs and configurations to generate evidence that supports ongoing compliance and control over installed applications. Evidence collection To collect evidence for monitoring and controlling installed applications, focus on gathering technical evidence from systems and configurations. Evidence can be collected by reviewing and documenting the configurations and logs of relevant security tools and management systems. Review Mobile Device Management (MDM) configurations to ensure they enforce application policies. Document application whitelisting/blacklisting policies and verify their implementation. name: Web Filtering Capabilities
evidenceGuidance: Provide evidence that demonstrates that your organization has implemented web filtering controls to reduce the risk of personnel accessing websites that contain illegal content, viruses, or phishing materials. This includes blocking access to known or suspected malicious websites, command and control servers, and websites sharing illegal content. Where to find the web filtering evidence: Web Protection in Anti-malware Solutions: Many small businesses already use anti-malware or antivirus software that includes basic web filtering features. If the company has an Anti-malware Solution, it likely has built-in Web Protection or Web Filtering. Where to check: Open the anti-malware software dashboard. Look for sections like Web Protection, Safe Browsing, or Web Control. This will typically list blocked websites or threats encountered during browsing. Capture screenshots of the enabled web filtering settings or download a report from the software. 2) Firewall or Router Settings: If the company uses a business-grade firewall or router (e.g., Cisco, SonicWall, or even certain Netgear routers), web filtering can often be configured directly within these devices. Where to check: Access the firewall or router’s admin panel. Look for sections like URL Filtering, Content Filtering, or Web Filtering. Capture screenshots of the settings and any activity logs showing blocked website attempts. 3) Browser-Based Protections: Modern browsers (like Chrome, Firefox, and Edge) come with built-in protection against dangerous websites. Where to check: In Chrome, go to Settings > Privacy and Security > Security. Check for “Safe Browsing” settings. Capture screenshots of this setting enabled. Implementation guidance Configure a web filtering control on your existing infrastructure (firewall, router, or anti-malware solution) by setting rules to block known malicious domains and content; document all settings and policy details. Test the implementation by accessing known test URLs (or safe simulated environments) to confirm the control's effectiveness, capturing screenshots of alerts or logs showing blocks. Set up automated logging and regular report generation from the filtering tools, then compile periodic evidence (screenshots, configuration exports, and maintenance records) to continuously demonstrate your security posture. Evidence collection To collect evidence for web filtering controls, focus on gathering technical evidence that demonstrates the effectiveness of these controls in blocking malicious websites and content. Capture screenshots of anti-malware solution dashboards showing blocked threats. Document firewall or router settings that specify web filtering rules. Obtain logs or reports from browser-based protection tools indicating blocked access to harmful sites. Compile records of regular updates and maintenance of web filtering systems.

name: Secure engineering principles defined

A template can be found here: Google docs template Implementation guidance Collaborate with engineering, product, and security teams to outline your guiding principles. Reference controls and lifecycle practices from NIST SP 800-160v1r1 or similar standards. Create a practical guide that applies each principle across phases like architecture design, threat modeling, dependency management, secure coding, peer review, and release. Approve the Secure Engineering Principles & Planning document through your change management or security governance process. Review it annually or when major architectural changes occur. Communicate and train engineers on how to apply the principles in their day-to-day work. Evidence collection To collect evidence for this control, gather a finalized document that clearly outlines the organization's secure engineering principles and planning methodology: Obtain the Secure Engineering Principles & Planning document. name: Security integration tests
evidenceGuidance: Provide evidence demonstrating the implementation of automated security testing within your application or infrastructure, including Static Application Security Testing (SAST), Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST), and Software Composition Analysis (SCA).Acceptable evidence and implementation guidance: Documentation of Security Testing Procedures: Outline your organization's approach to integrating automated security tests, specifying the tools used (e.g., GitHub Advanced Security, OWASP ZAP) and the frequency of these tests. CI/CD Pipeline Integration Evidence: Show how security testing tools are incorporated into your continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipeline, ensuring that code is automatically scanned for vulnerabilities during development. Access to Security Dashboards: Offer access to dashboards or platforms where ongoing security testing results are displayed, demonstrating continuous monitoring and management of security risks. Training Records: Document training sessions or materials provided to development teams on the importance and implementation of automated security testing practices. Create a simple reference guide that outlines which tools are used, how they are configured, and where results are stored. Save example scan reports and screenshots of dashboards to demonstrate coverage and activity. Provide basic training to your developers and engineers on how to interpret scan results and address findings. Review your testing setup regularly to ensure it stays aligned with changes in code, dependencies, or infrastructure. Evidence collection Evidence for this control would be collected by demonstrating how automated security testing is implemented and maintained within your application or infrastructure, specifically covering Static Application Security Testing (SAST), Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST), and Software Composition Analysis (SCA). Document the organization’s security testing procedures, including tools used, test types, frequency, and responsible teams. Offer access to or screenshots of security dashboards that display ongoing results, trends, or alerting mechanisms related to automated security scans. Collect training records or materials provided to developers or engineering teams on secure coding practices and use of automated testing tools. Ensure all evidence maps clearly to SAST, DAST, and SCA activities, with distinctions made for each category to support audit traceability.

name: Mobile code checked for vulnerabilities

name: Outsourced development contract
evidenceGuidance: Provide documented evidence demonstrating that the organization directs, monitors, and reviews outsourced system development activities. Corrective actions or follow-ups directed to the outsourced development team to address identified risks or non-compliance issues. Implementation guidance Outline key security, quality, and compliance standards needed in contracts or SLAs with third-party developers. Establish scheduled checkpoints (meetings or reports) to review performance, and plan regular technical assessments to verify adherence to the standards. Begin collecting and archiving contracts, reports, review outcomes, and records of any corrective actions. This documentation will serve as evidence for ongoing management of outsourced development activities. Review contracts or SLAs with third-party developers to ensure they include security, quality, and compliance standards. Gather records of oversight, such as status reports or meeting minutes, to demonstrate ongoing management. Collect results from security assessments or code reviews, along with any corrective actions taken to address identified risks or non-compliance.

name: Production data not used for dev or test
description: Production data not used for dev or test
evidenceGuidance: Screenshots, processes/procedures, or other evidence of how production data is prevented from being used, or validated to not be used for test and development environments Implementation guidance Create clear policies and procedures: Document rules that explicitly prohibit using production data in development or test environments. This should include guidelines on how data is classified and rules for data masking or anonymization when moving data between environments. Implement technical measures: Configure systems to enforce environment separation. Use data masking or synthetic data generation tools that automatically substitute production data when used in non-production settings, and ensure audit logging is enabled to track any access or transfers. Monitor and train: Establish regular reviews of audit logs and processes to verify compliance with the policies. Provide training sessions and materials to ensure staff understand and follow these controls, reinforcing the importance of data protection and compliance. Evidence collection To collect evidence that production data is not used in development or testing environments, focus on documentation that outlines processes and procedures. Obtain process documents or policies that explicitly state the prohibition of using production data in non-production environments. Gather screenshots or records from data masking tools or systems that demonstrate the implementation of data protection measures. Review audit logs or reports that verify compliance with the stated procedures. Collect any training materials or records that show staff awareness and adherence to these data handling policies.
